title: Gate CI and releases on a full book walk; fix checkpoint transitions
body:
Adds a full-book walk through the compiled CLI in persistent learner workspaces and makes it a gate for pull requests, main, and releases. The workflow installs the book runtimes, verifies every authored step, smoke-tests Python and JavaFX windows, and uploads a JSON report.

- Reconcile generated files between project checkpoints while preserving learner edits; update the content pin and Java checkpoint cleanup.
- Show program failures in the native learner and include command diagnostics for replay mismatches. Restrict relaxed replay output matching to the book-walk harness while retaining exit-code and timeout checks.
- Add regression coverage, Docker graphical test dependencies, and bump the CLI to 0.13.2.

Validation in this environment:

- Passed: content synchronization, TypeScript checking, local binary build/version smoke check, shell lint, and diff whitespace check.
- Passed: `bun run explore:learn:pr` — 1,100 cases, no findings.
- Full-book walk completed with failures: 94/163 steps passed, 2 failed, 67 not run after the failures; both graphical smoke checks passed. `java-6-15` fails because its Byte Buddy dependency does not support Java 27. `py-5-04` fails because the earlier generated `math.py` shadows the Python standard module. title: test: walk every authored book step in persistent workspaces

<!-- tracetoon:start -->

`test:books` runs the harness in `scripts/walk-books.ts`: authored steps in order, persistent book workspaces, headless external-launch replays and Pygame/JavaFX window smokes.
It accepts `--binary` (platform asset under `bin`, falling back to `bin/aifirst`), `--report` (default `test-results/book-walk/report.json`), `--book`, `--from`, `--skip-smoke`, and `--keep-workspace`; value flags read the following argument when present.

A reusable Ubuntu workflow installs learner runtimes, builds the binary, runs under Xvfb and uploads its report even after failure; PR/main CI invokes it, and tagged releases now depend on it alongside existing build and compatibility jobs.
The Docker test image includes graphical runtimes, and book-walk reports are ignored.

title: fix: use Homebrew for Maven on immutable Linux
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
The reported Bazzite error blocks `java-11-01` at Maven installation because Fedora Atomic rejects the package-manager operation. This PR addresses the request to detect immutable distributions and install Maven through Homebrew, so learners can prepare the Java exercise using an available supported installer. Previously, Maven installation plans selected Homebrew on macOS and offered APT, DNF, or Alpine apk branches on Linux.

For Linux, `isImmutableLinux` recognizes either `/run/ostree-booted` or an available `rpm-ostree` command; its default command lookup normalizes `Bun.which` results to `undefined` when missing. When Maven planning detects that environment and Homebrew is available, it selects the resolved Homebrew executable and runs `install maven` before considering the Linux package-manager branches. If Homebrew cannot be found, the planner returns no plan instead of falling through to DNF. When installation has no plan, the missing system dependencies consist of Maven, and immutable Linux is detected, the caller returns instructions to install Homebrew, put `brew` on PATH, and retry. Learners in that case receive an actionable prerequisite message rather than another DNF installation attempt.

`test/dependencies.test.ts` covers both detection signals, Homebrew selection on rpm-ostree systems, and refusal to fall through to DNF without Homebrew. The verification guide asks maintainers to approve Maven installation with supported package managers, verify `mvn`, and run the replay in Docker, with an additional rpm-ostree check for Homebrew preference and the missing-Homebrew case; the package version advances to `0.10.3`.

CI results for the final head are not present in the session logs.

title: fix: make Claude integration independent of aifirst on PATH
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Windows Claude Code hooks and exercise commands could fail with `aifirst: command not found`; this PR implements the requested durable fix across hooks, generated instructions, and permissions by installing a Claude-owned Bash launcher that delegates to the current CLI executable. Previously, the replay hook ran `aifirst replay hook`, permission rules used bare `aifirst` prefixes, and generated instructions embedded bare CLI commands.

The launcher quotes its executable arguments and forwards caller arguments; Windows drive paths become Git Bash paths, while other platforms retain normalized paths. Runtime detection normalizes the executable basename and preserves an absolute source entrypoint when the executable is Bun and the entry matches `src/index` with a supported JavaScript or TypeScript extension; otherwise the launcher invokes the executable alone. Claude installation renders the skill and slash-command bodies through this launcher and installs a marker-owned replay hook, recognizing both legacy bare hooks and marker-suffixed hooks during migration.

Permission grants replace known legacy entries with launcher-prefixed entries while retaining unrelated permissions; permission status and book mode's preapproval check require the launcher-prefixed set, and revocation recognizes both forms. The replay guide explains the stale Windows PATH issue and launcher-based replay command; existing users can refresh with `aifirst skill install --claude`, including the documented default executable path when PowerShell cannot yet resolve the command. Generated guidance sends native Windows users, including Git Bash users, to the PowerShell installer, sends macOS, Linux, and WSL users to the shell installer, and asks users to restart Claude Code and its terminal or editor host after installation.

`test/agents.test.ts` covers path conversion, argument quoting, source versus compiled invocation, forwarding scripts, and target-specific instructions; `test/permissions.test.ts` covers legacy permission migration and revocation without disturbing unrelated entries.

When Bash is available, `test/upgrade.test.ts` invokes the installed launcher with `PATH=/nonexistent` and checks stderr, exit status, and version output.

title: fix: defer macOS setup outside piped installer
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
macOS users reported being unable to answer `Set up 2 tools? [Y/n]` during installation; this PR implements the requested safe workaround and smoke test while waiting for a durable fix in a release. When setup is enabled on macOS, the installer prints instructions to open a new terminal and run `aifirst init`, moving that interaction outside the piped installer. The README explains this temporary extra step alongside the immediate guided setup on Linux and Windows.

With `AIFIRST_SKIP_SETUP=1`, the setup block remains skipped; otherwise, non-macOS systems with an accessible `/dev/tty` retain the direct setup invocation. For macOS installations where setup is enabled, users must run the follow-up command to enter guided setup. The installer comment attributes the workaround to Bun’s handling of stdin reopened through macOS’s `/dev/tty` alias and says direct invocation inherits the real terminal device.

The macOS smoke script requires a Darwin host and an executable binary argument, rejecting other platforms or invalid arguments with exit status 2. It supplies a local binary and checksum through a curl replacement, runs the piped installer in a pseudo-terminal, then invokes setup directly. In the PTY child, the driver executes the shell runner; in the parent, it answers the confirmation prompt with `n` and checks for a successful child exit. Missing prompts, abnormal or nonzero child exits, a timeout, missing completion markers, or a prompt appearing before installer completion cause the smoke check to fail.

CI invokes the smoke script on Darwin during build verification, and expands ShellCheck to cover the script; the macOS release build also invokes it. The session logs contain no run of the changed workflows. Recorded runs were on Linux, so they do not show the macOS smoke path running or the terminal interaction with a user at the keyboard.

title: feat: keep learner TUI responsive during program execution
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Long-running commands should not freeze rendering or force learners out of the TUI: this implements the requested “TUI Quality-of-Life Improvements” with live program output, embedded reader input, and faster prompt and plan reveal. Previously the asynchronous replay path delegated non-shell commands to the synchronous runner, and native exercise execution parsed output from a nested CLI invocation.

Terminal exercises now stream stdout/stderr into the TUI; interactive exercises expose an input field, with Ctrl+D closing attached stdin and Esc/Ctrl+C requesting cancellation. The shared execution path stops a command sequence on a nonzero exit, timeout, or abort. The standalone run command still rejects interactive steps without authored stdin when no terminal is attached; reader input uses an embedded callback when supplied and inherited stdin otherwise, while `noTimeout` disables the execution timeout; the final interactive command in reader-input mode also has no timeout.

Expected exceptions can still count as successful runs when the final command exits nonzero with stdout, without timing out or being aborted.

During prompt animation, an ordinary key or click reveals the remaining text and consumes that event, while Esc and Ctrl+C retain back/exit handling; plan animation also supports immediate reveal. Animation loops stop when skipped, and a run confirmation or accepted menu selection restores bottom-following. Detailed pickers reserve space for input hints and keep details in a compact panel with PageUp/PageDown scrolling when details exist.

Non-shell replay commands use asynchronous execution with the operation's working directory and stdin; unresolved `<python>` commands report runtime unavailability, and graphical launches are skipped on Linux without DISPLAY or WAYLAND_DISPLAY. Recognized PNGs produce metadata with dimensions; other reads containing NUL bytes or invalid UTF-8 produce metadata with dimensions unknown. Process input is piped for supplied or interactive input, timeout exits use code 124, and cancellation uses taskkill on Windows or process-group signals with a direct-process fallback elsewhere. Native execution reports stopped programs when execution returns `aborted`; verification commands show an animated task panel using the operation's display title when provided. The package version advances from 0.13.3 to 0.13.4.

`test/graphical-run.test.ts` covers streaming output and reader input inside the TUI, while `test/replay-flow.test.ts` covers nonblocking commands, timeouts, and PNG metadata.

The TUI displays its no-console-output message when neither program output nor echoed input was displayed.

Recorded renderer tests use fakes or stubs; recorded Linux runs do not show Windows cancellation, and recorded nonterminal checks do not show standalone interactive handling with a person at the keyboard. Final-head CI results are absent from the session logs.

title: fix: make Python replay commands portable across platforms
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR adds a portable shell representation for captured Python replay commands and normalizes matching Python invocations while preserving tool labels and command text for playback, preparing the content for the requested “commit, push, and release.” Previously, the importer emitted executable shell commands as `bash -lc` argv without the separate portable command and display fields.

For imported command operations whose source paths include a `.py` file, the importer retains the captured execution argv and supplies `portableCommand` beginning with `<shell>`; matching `python3` invocations become `<python>`. Display metadata uses the original tool name, falling back to `Tool` when the tool name is nullish, and includes description and command input strings when they are truthy. This separates playback presentation from the execution representation, including the original PowerShell label in the Python content.

The replay types and schema support optional display metadata on operations and status events, with a required nonempty `toolName` when display metadata is present; command operations also accept portable argv and timeout settings. Validation rejects an explicitly empty portable command and an expected timeout without `timeoutMs`. For Python steps, a captured `bash` command containing the checked Python, `rm`, `timeout`, `ls`, or environment-assignment patterns must provide a portable command starting with `<shell>`; that requirement propagates through replay events, pre-plan events, workflow interludes, and variants. Content maintainers therefore get a validation error for these shell-dependent Python commands when the portable representation is missing.

The Rocket replay fixture also pairs captured commands with portable argv and display metadata.

The Python book’s captured command records gain portable argv and display metadata, including availability checks such as `<python> --version; <python> -c "import pygame; print(pygame.ver)"`; the package version advances from `1.7.1` to `1.7.2`. `test/python-chapters-9-10-audit.test.ts` checks portable execution for captured shell commands and preservation of the Windows tool label separately from execution.

title: fix: record starting scaffolds for independent exercise replays
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
The unavailable chapter 9 project state in an independent `py-10-01` replay motivates the request for exercises that work “independently of each other.” This PR records the starting exercise scaffold needed by a captured replay, so consumers can identify the project state that its operations expect. Previously, `processBundle` supplied the preceding exercise’s scaffold files to derivation without passing that exercise’s ID.

The importer now carries that ID alongside the preceding scaffold when initial files and a preceding exercise are available, preferring the step ID and falling back to the parent ID. Derivation examines pre-plan events, workflow interludes, and completion events for a read or edit of a path supplied by the initial scaffold before that path has been created during the replay. The detector returns false for missing or empty initial files, skips non-operation events, and tracks write and edit paths as created. When a starting exercise ID is supplied and that dependency is detected, the replay receives `initialState.fromExercise`.

The optional field is represented in the TypeScript replay type and JSON schema; when present, its object requires a nonempty `fromExercise` string and rejects extra properties. The Python progression records the preceding state across the chapter 9 and chapter 10 continuation exercises, including `py-10-01` starting from `py-9-03`. Content validation rejects a referenced exercise that cannot be found or has no scaffold files, giving maintainers a gate against unusable starting-state references. Consumers therefore gain an explicit prerequisite scaffold reference for these continuations, while derivation leaves the field absent when its ID or detected dependency is missing.

`test/chapter10-retrofit.test.ts` asserts that captured replays link to their preceding project state, and `test/chapter9-retrofit.test.ts` asserts the captured starting exercise for standalone fallback.

title: fix(digest): distinguish shell commands from quoted script text
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR addresses false test-run detection when an inline script contains text such as `bun test`, supporting the request to “dogfood this and use it for a PR.” Previously command consumers split on shell separators without tracking quotes or heredoc bodies, misclassifying embedded runner text, and the release version was `1.0.0-rc.11`. A shared splitter now supplies command segments to test detection, grouping and commit detection, so those consumers can distinguish inline script text from the surrounding command chain.

`splitCommands` tracks single, double and backtick quotes; outside quotes it splits chains and pipes, while backslash escapes preserve the following character outside single quotes. When it recognizes a heredoc delimiter and a following newline, it skips the body through a matching terminator, or through the end of the input if none is found, then resumes splitting commands that follow. Quoted strings remain within their enclosing command rather than becoming independent candidates for detection.

For digest consumers, `testSegment` applies runner detection to these segments, and `commandKey` uses them to find the first command after setup commands. Grouping also filters tokens beginning with `-`, `<`, `>`, or a digit followed by `>` before selecting the program and first argument. Commit detection uses the same segmentation before checking for commit-making commands. This gives callers consistent boundaries for quoted scripts and recognized heredocs across the three consumers.

The splitter’s comment motivates this handling by noting that agents often run scripts inline; the commit message gives `bun test',` as an example of a malformed grouping key and identifies this as fixing a known gap noted in PR #8.

`tests/shell.test.ts` covers chains and pipes, quoted scripts, commands following heredoc bodies, test-runner text inside scripts and grouping by the real first command; release metadata and the generated bundle accompany version `1.0.0-rc.12`.

title: fix(digest): ground summaries in the work belonging to each PR
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR aims to “see if summaries are being generated properly with tracetoon first”: it tightens which work reaches a digest and puts its evidence beside the description for review.

Previously, committed work used a window ending 30 minutes after the last commit, or at the current time for a dirty checkout; commit recognition depended on SHA output, and test failures depended on the command error flag.

For PRs with commits, the window now ends five minutes after the last commit, including dirty checkouts. When a session contains a recognizable base-branch commit, its latest timestamp supplies a cutoff: turns finished before it lose their records except links and artifacts; crossing turns retain conversation while dropping earlier work. Quiet commits can match a `git commit` command's subject when that subject has at least 12 characters, and `.git` paths, including Tracetoon’s run files, are excluded from repository edits. Binary diff entries count as changed files, and callers supplying `head` can inspect a historical commit or branch without using working-tree changes.

Recognized test commands use their test-runner segment as the grouping label; failure patterns in test output also inform the failure count and subsequent recovery milestone. For errored Claude tool results, non-synthetic text after “the user said:” becomes feedback that continues the current turn. Saga relationships retain stacked branches and explicit links, dropping shared sessions as a relationship criterion.

The preview exposes facts, prompts, conditional plans and decisions, tests, milestones and disclosure, so reviewers can compare claims with digest evidence. The writing guide asks for sentence-by-sentence claim checks, sourced numbers and recorded plan approval. The evaluation harness rebuilds digests for six configured histories of real work with expected ground truth, reports PASS/FAIL from each check's boolean, writes digests and a report, and emits structured output with `--json`; the commit describes it as intended for local evaluation using machine-local logs. `tests/summary-fixes.test.ts` checks piped failures, runner labels, binary changes, rejection feedback and exclusion of earlier work; versions advance from 1.0.0-rc.5 to 1.0.0-rc.6.

This PR addresses the request for “a proper link that can be followed in a browser” and improves summary relevance while dogfooding Tracetoon. Previously, render and preview printed bare paths, command membership could follow the logged cwd before a leading directory change, and commit-output matching accepted a SHA without checking whether the command could create commits. Relative destinations require a cwd, home-relative paths expand, and Git Bash drive spelling is normalized on Windows. SHA-output matching now requires a recognized commit-making Git command (`commit`, `merge`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`, `am`, `rebase` or `pull`), including one inside a chain; the subject-based matching path remains. Previously, edits outside the repository could stretch an earlier turn past the cutoff and retain its prompts. title: Retry timed-out judges and account for Codex subagent costs
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Timed-out judge calls should be recoverable within the retry budget, and comparison reports should expose the usage and reliability behind their scores. Previously judge exceptions retried transient failures but stopped on timeouts, while Codex stdout supplied main-thread token counts. This PR extends retry handling and rollout accounting so resumable comparisons can retain their identity and report more complete costs.

The retry comment treats timeout and transient errors as unrelated to draft quality; these errors receive backoff within the three-attempt budget, including a persisted timeout on resume; cancellation still stops retries. Codex judge processes explicitly classify a timed-out execution before interpreting its exit code. Unsuccessful attempts retain the judge identity, and score output includes a per-judge breakdown of timeout, transient, format and other failures when those records exist.

Codex writers inspect rollouts created under the sandbox CODEX_HOME, deduplicate response IDs across replayed histories, and prefer their totals when they cover at least the stdout input-token count; otherwise stdout usage is labeled main-thread when inputTokens is available. Artifacts carry optional usage scope and subagent counts, with validation of the scope and nonnegative count. For Codex artifacts without a reported dollar cost, scoring can recover usage from saved traces from the newest numbered writer attempt without a failure record that has traces; cost coverage labels and mean subagents per draft make the accounting visible. Final-judgment discovery skips attempt folders to avoid counting accepted judgment copies, while paired comparisons gain per-case candidate-minus-same-model-baseline deltas and a leave-one-case-out range when at least two cases exist.

Probes now record the full arm specification (`model@effort`), and saved isolation proofs accept that identity with a bare-model fallback for older proofs. Writer environment hashes exclude shell and session bookkeeping for Codex and Claude (the code comment identifies this as shell-dependent context that does not affect writer behavior), while frozen experiments retain a matching legacy hash. The experiment identity still must match before an older proof can use the fallback.

title: Gate performance on paired priced cost per draft
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
A candidate can use more cached input and take longer while costing less; this PR implements the cost-based performance criterion so those runs can qualify on priced cost.
Previously, the gate required per-model median writer time to improve and median input tokens not to increase, with the writer-ratio interval also constraining a pass.

Performance report `prbench.performance/v3` pairs candidate and baseline drafts by model, case and replicate, averages log cost ratios within each case and then across cases, and uses a geometric mean ratio of at most 1.000 as its cost criterion.
The case-clustered 95% interval remains descriptive; a pass still requires complete pairs across at least two cases, usable validation comparison and required work evidence.
Writer wall time and token counts remain information, so a cheaper candidate may qualify despite slower execution or higher input usage.

Pricing is extracted from `collectDraftScores` into shared `draftCost`, which the comparison also uses: reported totals take precedence, otherwise estimates use model-specific prices and cached-input rates, matching `prbench score`.
For Codex estimates, all-thread artifact usage is preferred, with saved writer traces used when available and sufficiently complete; if no usable trace usage is found and input tokens are present, the estimate is marked main-thread.
Missing priced cost, nonpositive or nonfinite cost, or an estimated cost covering just the main thread makes a paired draft unusable for the gate and is listed with its reason in the report and comparison summary, leaving the gate inconclusive.
Validation-comparability handling retains its existing effect, including the stated limitation when validation was unavailable to both writers across the pairs.
The comparison summary prints the rule, priced-cost ratio and interval, unpriced drafts, and writer ratio labeled as information.
README and changelog describe the v3 cost criterion and descriptive timing and token fields.

`tests/performance.test.ts` covers case clustering, cheaper-but-slower candidates with more input tokens, pricier-but-faster candidates, unpriced paired drafts and the stated threshold; `tests/comparison.test.ts` assertions check the v3 schema, rule, summary labels and priced-cost fields.

title: fix: recover shell exit codes from Claude result text
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR supports the request to “use the chapter 9 exercises as the acceptance criteria” by preserving shell exit codes encoded in Claude tool-result text, so imported results can retain that status for verification.

Previously, `rawToolResult` looked for integer exit codes in structured result fields and then the tool-result block’s `exitCode`, `exit_code`, or `code` fields, without consulting its text content. The fallback now reads the block’s `content` when neither numeric lookup supplies a value; structured numeric results therefore retain precedence over a status embedded in text.

The new `resultTextExitCode` helper accepts a leading `Exit code ` followed by an optionally negative integer, terminated by a newline, a Windows newline, or the end of the string. Empty content and text without that leading match yield no recovered code, and the parsed number must satisfy `Number.isInteger` before it is returned. Consequently, consumers of imported tool-result events can receive an `exitCode` from matching result text even when the numeric fields are absent.

The helper’s comment describes Claude encoding a shell failure status solely in result text.

In `tests/claudeToolCall.test.ts`, the existing Bash case gains a tool-result event assertion for `exitCode: 1` and `isError: true`, with `Exit code 1` prefixed to its fixture content.

title: feat: let installed Showtail copies upgrade themselves
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Installed Showtail copies need a direct update command so users do not have to find and re-run the installer, fulfilling the request to “Make a showtail upgrade command to upgrade showtail from an install.” This PR exposes `showtail upgrade` for standalone installs and selects the latest GitHub release asset for Linux/macOS x64 or arm64 and Windows x64, rejecting unsupported targets. Previously, the CLI handled integration arguments through its existing tool and option validation branches; the patch registers upgrade as a separate maintenance command.

The updater compares numeric release versions before downloading assets: when the installed version is current it reports that it is up to date, and when it is newer than the latest release it leaves the installation unchanged. For an available upgrade, it stages the executable and bundled VS Code extension beside the installed files, checks the downloaded executable’s reported version, and backs up the installed files before replacement, restoring them if replacement throws. Standalone executable validation rejects Bun/source invocations before release lookup, protecting the runtime executable from replacement; those users must continue updating through their package or Git workflow.

On Windows, replacement is deferred to a detached PowerShell helper that waits for the command to exit, swaps the files, and attempts to refresh integrations; the command reports a pending upgrade when that helper has been scheduled. On non-Windows installs, the replacement completes in the command and integration refresh is attempted afterward; if refresh fails, the output says integrations will refresh on the next run. The command also supports `--json`, and the README, changelog, CLI reference, installation guide, and classroom guidance describe the upgrade command.

`tests/selfUpgrade.test.ts` covers release asset mapping, numeric version comparison, Windows helper generation, executable rejection, replacement, current-version handling, and preservation on verification failure; `tests/cli.test.ts` covers rejecting a Bun/source invocation. Windows checks were reported running for hours; this PR addresses the request to “fix the remaining issues in a branch” by bounding unfinished test processes and keeping fork publication tied to a resolved repository.

Repository resolution prefers gh’s default when it matches a clone remote, otherwise origin; without origin it can use the default, while offline resolution avoids gh.

Repository-specific lookups use the resolved target; doctor checks push access on origin when known, falling back to the target, and automatic private-repository attachment decisions use the target while image hosting remains on origin.

title: Run planned PR reviews together and merge their findings
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR supports the request to “put a plan together for the next code round” by making parallel reviewer reviews feed one correction round; the earlier analysis identified errors introduced when reviewer fixes were copied word for word. Previously the skill instructed drafters to run `review run` once per lens and then recheck; it now directs one `review run --all`, one merged list and one edit pass, with rechecks following the configured setting.

`review run --all` schedules one pass per lens plus general reviews beyond the lens count, concurrently, with separate packet, reply, findings and reviewed-body files for each slot. If a pass fails, successful reviews remain imported, unsuccessful reviews and a rerun command are reported, and the command exits nonzero; reruns preserve reviews already imported for the current body on the verified model unless `--fresh` is supplied. A single run without `--lens` also accepts plans that need general reviews beyond their lenses.

`review run --all` and `review merge` write `review-findings-merged.md`, which trims quotes and fixes, combines normalized or near-duplicate quotes, and matches findings without quotes by kind and matching nonempty evidence sets; evidence accepts arrays or comma/pipe-separated strings. Near-duplicate matching requires at least three distinct words unless normalized quotes match exactly. It retains the strongest verdict, puts claim verdicts before missing findings, names contributing reviews, caps the list at 12, and excludes claim quotes absent from the current render. `review merge` provides that list for agent-imported reviews.

`Review recheck: once|contested|none` and `prepare --review-recheck` select correction guidance, defaulting to `once` and storing nondefault values in the plan. With `--all --recheck`, prior reviews resume; `contested` selects reviews with retained flagged claims after a body change, and `--note` forwards supplied rejection notes, including supporting diff lines. Prepare, render and skill instructions follow this setting, while rechecks remain advice rather than a publish requirement.

title: fix: recognise VEX AIM user serial ports and complete user writes
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR addresses the request to fix “the bug with the serial ports on the vex aim devices” by recognising the AIM user interface and completing writes made through a dedicated user port. Previously, location-based discovery used the V5 Brain interface layout (system 0, user 2), dropped AIM interface 4, and returned `Some(empty)` when it recognised nothing; the dedicated-user write path issued a single write that could accept part of the buffer, returned that count, and did not flush.

In `types_by_location()`, for AIM devices with PID `0x0700`, location-based discovery now classifies interface 4 as a user port, while preserving the existing system/interface-0 and Brain user/interface-2 mappings. The recognition commit explains that AIM interfaces 2 and 3 belong to its UVC camera, which accounts for the different serial interface layout. When `types_by_location()` recognises no ports, it returns `None`; the recognition commit describes this as enabling name-based fallbacks in `find_ports()`. The recognition commit describes the prior consequence as `find_devices()` returning no user port and `read_user()`/`write_user()` using the system-port fallback; recognising interface 4 addresses that discovery gap.

When a dedicated user port exists, `write_user()` now uses `write_all()`, flushes, and returns the buffer length after those operations succeed; the existing system-port fallback remains in the other branch. The write-fix commit describes the complete-write-and-flush sequence as matching the existing system-port `send()` behavior.

The added unit tests in `packages/vex-v5-serial/src/serial.rs` cover AIM interfaces 0/4, Brain interfaces 0/2, and unrecognised locations returning `None`. Their input helper adjusts interface numbers on macOS to match the discovery code’s existing subtraction of one. title: Add AIM REPL probes and experimental file upload tools
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR provides AIM REPL round-trip probes and experimental file operations, making it possible to inspect files, upload a slot payload, and request a run or stop through separate commands. The commit message describes finding the AIM REPL on USB interface 4 and reports 10/10 round trips.

tests/pingpong.py takes a serial port and optional iteration count, defaulting to 10, and sends a Python print expression whose echoed source differs from the expected PONG output. A round trip succeeds when the response contains the PONG line followed by the REPL prompt within two seconds; the script emits JSON with per-trip success and latency, including received bytes for unsuccessful trips. tests/repl.py sends CRLF-terminated expressions and prints their responses, while tests/capture.py records incoming bytes and optionally sends supplied lines after four seconds, using the EOL environment variable when set.

The file commands select the first discovered device. aimupload writes slot_N.ini followed by slot_N.bin to the User vendor’s QSPI target with DoNothing exit actions; metadata includes a timestamp and version 1.0.0.0, and the payload type defaults to Vm unless the third argument is bin. Callers must invoke aimload to request execution: run defaults to slot_1.bin, while stop sends the name null. dirlist visits six vendor namespaces, continues after count errors, and requests at most 64 entries per namespace.

The uploader documents `aimupload <file> <slot 1-8> [vm|bin]`, but parses the slot as u8 without enforcing 1–8, and computes the INI slot as slot - 1.

An INI upload can remain if the subsequent binary upload fails. Its comments describe the format as a hypothesis based on cargo-v5 PR#22 and VAIMRC-Console and label the experiment instructor-approved with an exclusive robot; aimload’s comment attributes the null convention to VAIMRC-Console.

The probe dependency enables file-commands alongside serial with default features disabled, and the reference gitlinks pin VAIMRC-Console to b645a6e and aim-ai to 38b1b9b. Generated build/pingpong-run1.json, build/run1.log, build/run2.log and the dependency lockfile accompany the tools.

title: Make tag search stationary and add opt-in fast contact play
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Make pickup-and-delivery games brisk enough for children by supporting the requested assume-and-continue play, while preserving explicit diagnostic verification. The controller combines stationary tag views with opt-in `verification="contact"`, so scripts can continue after a bounded contact attempt without treating assumed pickup or placement as native confirmation. Previously collection required possession confirmation and retention verification, and delivery required confirmed cargo before placement.

Tag targets use up to eight stopped viewpoints, 45 degrees apart in the requested direction, settling for 300 ms before taking up to three native readings with 100 ms pauses between unsuccessful samples. Search stops advancing after the eighth view or when the elapsed search time reaches 20 seconds; the shared activity deadline also applies. `tag_turn_dps` controls travel between views and defaults to the configured turn speed. Tag reacquisition also pauses 300 ms before sampling; cargo search retains its continuous sweep.

In contact mode, a held-cargo reading can satisfy collection, or selected nearby cargo can proceed through bounded contact without a retention reverse; the local contact limit may end the attempt, while the activity deadline still applies. During marker approach, possession-loss checks apply in vision mode. Delivery accepts the same activity's remembered contact pickup, while standalone delivery still requires confirmed cargo, and the pre-placement possession gate applies in vision mode. Assumed outcomes report `completed: true` with nullable `collected` or `delivered` and explicit evidence, allowing subsequent effects without claiming physical confirmation.

The bundled guidance tells agents to follow workshop contact settings when applicable and accept assumed routine completion without host camera verification; explicit diagnostics retain the default vision policy, with matching release inputs and the behavior guide requirement advancing from 0.5.0 to 0.5.1. `dev/test_behaviors.py` covers stationary search in both directions, absent markers, missing possession readings, bounded contact, missing cargo, assumed release and deadline enforcement using a simulated world. Short native moves receive a minimum 1,500 ms limit and return early on completion; the short-reverse simulation checks acceleration margin.

title: Prefer SDL FreeRDP for full Windows desktops on Wayland
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Full Windows desktop launches on Wayland should use SDL FreeRDP while keeping the upstream change minimal: the request was to “prefer the simplest change that will get the intended result,” including unversioned SDL binaries and the Flatpak case. Previously automatic command selection preferred `xfreerdp`, with native and Flatpak alternatives following that path. On Wayland sessions, this PR prefers SDL FreeRDP, including the FreeRDP Flatpak, for the full Windows desktop view when automatic selection applies. `waGetFreeRDPCommand` receives the launch argument to distinguish `windows` from application launches.

When `FREERDP_COMMAND` is empty, the launch argument is `windows`, and `XDG_SESSION_TYPE` is `wayland`, selection tries `sdl-freerdp3`, then `sdl3-freerdp`, then `sdl-freerdp`, taking the first command available on `PATH`. If those native commands are absent and Flatpak lists `com.freerdp.FreeRDP`, it selects `flatpak run --command=sdl-freerdp com.freerdp.FreeRDP` and sets `RDP_FLATPAK=1`. The command acceptance condition also recognizes that exact SDL Flatpak invocation, allowing it to reach the existing handling of configured RDP flags.

For users with several native SDL executable names installed, that ordering determines which client a Wayland full desktop launch selects; an explicit `FREERDP_COMMAND` bypasses automatic selection. If the SDL branch leaves the command empty, selection continues through the existing X11 client candidates, and automatic selection for RemoteApp and other application launches retains the existing path.

Windows compiled executables crashed even when the standalone Bun runtime worked; this PR prepares the release pipeline for SignPath Foundation approval and implements the request to “change to Apache 2.0 instead of MIT.” The design combines native Windows builds with PE metadata checks, explicit licensing, and a pending signing configuration while Windows releases remain unsigned during the application process.

The pending SignPath configuration identifies the x64, baseline x64, and arm64 Windows executables and their expected product name, versions, company, and copyright.

Apache licensing, attribution, and trademark terms accompany policy disclosures covering project roles, privacy, system changes, and release integrity; sensitive release paths gain CODEOWNERS coverage, while workflows use Bun 1.4.0 and the Claude Code compatibility pin becomes 2.1.252. To address the execution problem in Java exercise `6-05`, this PR adds the content-side ordered book-walk harness and project checkpoints requested to expose problems caused by earlier exercises in shared workspaces. The content harness retains isolated verification and adds an ordered pass with persistent workspaces per book. For steps with both a project root and response path, the ordered pass removes previously tracked project files absent from the next checkpoint and applies declared cleanup paths before verification. title: fix: make Python replay commands portable across platforms

<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Python replays need portable execution while retaining the captured tool presentation; this PR separates executable argv from display metadata to support that purpose. Previously, imported shell operations stored `bash -lc` commands, while status text selected a description, name, or prompt to label a tool.

The importer replaces supported `python3` invocations with `<python>` and records the original tool name, falling back to `Tool`, plus a description and command when those fields are present. For Python steps, the portability requirement reaches operations, replay events, pre-plan events, workflow interludes, and variants: captured Bash commands matching the Python, removal, timeout, listing, or environment-assignment patterns must supply a `<shell>` portable command. Content authors therefore receive a validation error for those Python shell operations when the portable representation is missing.

title: fix(digest): distinguish shell commands from quoted script text
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
The request to “dogfood this and use it for a PR” motivates fixing command detection so inline script text does not become a detected test command. Previously command detection split on shell separators even inside quoted scripts and heredoc bodies, which could count an embedded `bun test` line as a test command. The new `splitCommands` helper supplies command segments to test detection, command grouping, and commit detection.

The splitter tracks single quotes, double quotes, and backticks, keeping separators inside those quoted spans with their surrounding command; it preserves escaped character pairs outside quotes and inside quotes other than single quotes. Outside those spans it splits chains and pipes at `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, and newlines. When it recognizes a heredoc opener with a supported delimiter and finds the following newline, it skips the body through the closing delimiter, or through the remaining input if that delimiter is missing. Commands following a closed heredoc remain available for detection rather than being discarded with its body.

For callers, a runner name embedded in the covered quoted-script and heredoc cases stays text, while a following test command can still be identified. Grouping keys also filter tokens beginning with flags, heredoc markers, or redirection prefixes before selecting the program and first argument; the release metadata moves from 1.0.0-rc.11 to 1.0.0-rc.12 with a regenerated bundle. `tests/shell.test.ts` covers chains and pipes, quoted scripts, heredoc continuation, embedded runner names, and grouping from the first command.

title: fix(digest): evaluate summary accuracy and expose supporting evidence
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
To support the stated goal to “see if summaries are being generated properly”, this PR improves summary evaluation by tightening which work enters a digest and making its supporting facts visible beside the description.
Previously, committed-work windows ended 30 minutes after the last commit, or at the current time for a dirty checkout; they now end five minutes after the last commit when commits exist.

When a session can be matched to a base-branch commit with a valid timestamp, its latest such timestamp becomes the earlier-work cutoff: turns whose work ended by that cutoff are dropped, while crossing turns retain conversation and lose earlier work records, with links and artifacts exempt.
Git-internal paths are excluded from repo edits, binary diff entries count as changed files, and commit subjects of at least 12 characters can match commit commands even without SHA output.
An explicit head lets evaluations inspect a past commit or branch without including the checkout’s working tree.

The digest labels recognized test commands by their test runner rather than the first command; `testOutputFailed` reads recognized failure output, including piped runs, and a later nonfailed test record can produce a recovery milestone.
Claude rejection text becomes feedback when an error tool result contains nonsynthetic user text, keeping that feedback within the current turn.
Saga relationships retain stacked branches and explicit PR links but discard shared-session matching as a relationship criterion.

The evaluation script defines six historical cases and privacy assertions for comparing digests with expected prompts, milestones, files and counts, writes digest reports, and prints PASS/FAIL assertions as text by default or structured results with `--json`; the commit message describes this harness as intended for local use.
The preview’s Evidence section shows digest facts, prompts, conditional plans and decisions, tests, milestones and disclosure, using foreground text and muted annotations.
The writing guide asks for a claim-by-claim evidence check before rendering, alongside the rc.6 version and rebuilt bundle.
Reviewers can therefore compare description claims with the displayed digest before publication.

title: Support focused comparison runs and cross-model composite deltas

To help find defaults that deliver “the same or higher score and much lower cost,” this PR lets comparison runs omit native writers and exposes the composite difference needed to compare candidate and baseline models.
Previously, comparison execution and rebuilding used baseline and native as the candidate’s comparison opponents.

`compare --systems` accepts comma-separated `native`, `baseline`, and `candidate` aliases, full Tracetoon system names, and the selected provider’s native name; omitting it selects all three systems.
Selection is normalized into the provider’s canonical order, and unknown names or selections missing baseline or candidate are rejected; the code comment describes the baseline pairing as the primary comparison.
With `--systems baseline,candidate`, native writers are omitted and candidate-versus-baseline judgments run in both orders.
Planned writer and judgment counts, rebuild coverage, the quality gate, and `--plan` output (including `systems` and `judgedAgainst`) follow the selected systems, so callers can budget a two-system experiment without a native comparison requirement.

A subset is stored in manifest settings and participates in experiment identity; selecting all three leaves the systems field absent to preserve the previous identity.
When resuming without `--systems`, the run retains its frozen selection; manifests without a systems field use the provider’s full system list.
`tests/comparison.test.ts` covers three-system execution, two-system planning, completion, scoring, resume behavior, and rejection of missing required or unknown systems, but these tests use `fakeComparisonSetup` rather than the real comparison setup.

When candidate and baseline arms have shared cases, the accuracy view includes composite delta alongside error-rate delta, claims, the coverage guard, and cost ratio.
The delta is candidate minus baseline over per-case means, with a case-clustered 95% bootstrap interval; `tests/score.test.ts` checks clustering and reproducibility.

title: Compare saved drafts across writer-model runs with crossjudge
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
To help “confirm the Haiku win” with direct comparisons rather than composites from separate runs, this PR introduces `crossjudge`: it pairs saved `tracetoon-candidate` drafts from one comparison run with saved `tracetoon-baseline` drafts from another, including runs with different writer models.

The command reuses draft artifacts rather than running writers, then judges each case/replicate pair in both orders with each configured judge and applies compare’s consensus rule. Previously the existing compare CLI set exit code 1 when its result had pending work; the separate crossjudge command catches errors with exit code 2.

Callers supply `--candidate`, `--baseline` and `--out`; `--plan` verifies inputs and prints planned pair/call counts without calling models, while `--parallel` defaults to 4 and must be a positive integer at the CLI. `--cache` overrides the default cache at the output directory’s parent under `.prbench-cache/v2`; execution without `--plan` requires Claude authentication at the CLI.

Inputs must each identify exactly one writer model, and their judge contracts, judge lists, rubric versions, replicates, splits and case identities/hashes must match. The rubric and judge contract must also match the current harness; saved drafts are checked against their identities and receipts before judge calls begin, so missing drafts stop execution before spending on judging.

The output directory receives `pairs.json`, `summary.json` and `summary.md`; reports include consensus and per-judge tallies, per-case results, per-draft composite scores and factual-error rates, plus summed judge costs where stored costs are numeric. Inconclusive verdicts receive a separate tally, and completed pairs are saved in deterministic order even when a later job fails.

`tests/crossjudge.test.ts` covers cross-run pairing and consensus, refusal of mismatched judge contracts, judge lists, cases and replicates, and missing drafts before judge calls; these tests use fake judges rather than real judge services.

title: Retry timed-out judges and report Codex subagent costs accurately
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Timed-out judge calls should get another attempt, and comparison costs should include Codex subagents when their usage is available. Previously the judge retry loop continued for transient failures but stopped on timeouts, while draft scoring used artifact token metadata directly. This change retries timeout and transient failures with backoff within three attempts per order judgment, including resumed persisted timeouts; cancellation stops retries, and Codex process timeouts are reported explicitly. Maintainers can resume those interrupted comparisons without resetting the attempt budget.

Live Codex writers inspect newly created sandbox rollouts, deduplicate response IDs across replayed fork history, and prefer their summed usage when it covers at least stdout's input-token count; otherwise available stdout counts are marked main-thread. Usage scope and subagent counts propagate into artifact metadata, with schema validation restricting scope to the two supported values and subagent counts to nonnegative numbers. For Codex artifacts without a reported dollar cost, scoring uses all-thread metadata when present or tries retained traces located through the artifact receipt and writer attempts without failure records, accepting trace usage when its input count covers the artifact's count. Retained traces let older runs be rescored without new calls.

Reports label cost coverage and known subagents per draft, preserving reported dollar costs.

Scoring skips judgment-attempt directories so accepted copies do not duplicate final judgments, and paired composite deltas show per-case candidate-minus-baseline values by model plus a leave-one-case-out range when at least two cases are available, showing sensitivity to a single case. Malformed replies retain one format repair; unsuccessful judge attempts retain their judge identity; score output includes timeout, transient, format and other failure counts when failures exist, including comparison summaries and Markdown score CLI output.

Writer environment hashes exclude shell, terminal and session bookkeeping for Codex and Claude; frozen experiments retain a matching legacy hash when the current hash does not match. Previously isolation probes stored bare model names while resume compared full effort arms.

Isolation probes record the full arm specification, while saved proofs without it may match the bare model alongside existing experiment, digest, system and successful-probe checks.

title: Gate paired performance on priced cost per draft
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
The performance gate should reflect the cost-based decision: a candidate can use more cached input and take longer while costing less per draft. Previously, the gate required improved median paired writer time and rejected increased median input tokens, with the writer-ratio interval also affecting conclusiveness. This PR makes paired priced cost the performance criterion, while retaining writer wall time and token counts as information.

For matching model, case and replicate pairs, the report averages log cost ratios within each case, then across cases; the resulting candidate/baseline geometric mean must be at most 1.000 to meet the cost criterion when completeness, comparable validation and required work evidence permit a conclusive decision. The case-clustered 95% interval is reported as information. A paired draft with missing, nonfinite or nonpositive cost, or estimated Codex usage limited to its main thread, makes the gate inconclusive and is listed with its reason. 

`rebuildComparison` attaches priced cost to writer metrics and renders the rule, cost ratio and unpriced drafts alongside the informational writer ratio. Validation-comparability handling is unchanged.

Pricing is extracted into shared `draftCost`, which `collectDraftScores` and comparison rebuilding now call: reported totals take precedence; otherwise estimates use model-specific prices and cached-input rates. For Codex estimates, all-thread artifact usage or suitable saved traces supply usage when available; main-thread fallback is marked so the gate can reject incomplete pricing. Estimated costs use `src/report/prices.json` list prices rather than invoice amounts.

Callers therefore get the same cost basis as `prbench score`, and a cheaper candidate can pass despite slower writing or more input tokens.

`tests/performance.test.ts` covers case clustering, cheaper-but-slower candidates, pricier-but-faster candidates, missing pricing and the stated threshold; README and changelog describe the v3 cost rule.

`tests/comparison.test.ts` asserts the v3 schema, summary rule and ratio labels, and priced cost on writer metrics.

To “upgrade showtail from an install so users don't have to re-run the installer,” this PR adds `showtail upgrade` for standalone installations, fetching a compatible binary from the latest GitHub release and updating the bundled editor extension alongside it. On non-Windows platforms, replacement failures restore the staged backups; Windows uses a detached PowerShell helper that waits for the running command to exit before swapping the files and refreshing integrations, and attempts to restore staged backups if replacement fails. Bun/source invocations are refused before the release request, protecting the runtime path from replacement, so those users must continue updating through their package or Git workflow.

title: Guard CLI tests against lingering Bun processes and fix PR targeting
body:
## Summary

CLI subprocesses can finish their work yet leave Bun running on Windows, stalling tests and CI. Add a shared CLI spawn guard that preserves output and recorded exit status, flush CLI output before explicitly exiting, and redirect review-test subprocess output to files. Bound test files with a watchdog, allow a grace period after Bun prints its test summary, retain per-file logs, and set a 45-minute CI job timeout.

This branch also resolves one PR target repository, carries it through context and rendering, and passes it explicitly to GitHub operations. Publishing from a fork qualifies the head with its owner, while a target change after rendering blocks publication. Check receipts now contribute validation evidence without task bookkeeping; summaries prefer wrapper totals and receipt reuse ignores temporary-directory and terminal settings.

Includes regression coverage for the spawn guard, file watchdog, repository targeting, fork heads, and receipt handling, plus the rebuilt shipped bundle.

title: Bound hanging CLI tests and keep fork publication on its approved repository
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Windows checks were hanging for hours; this PR addresses “Is the windows check hung? 3 hours.” and the request to “fix the remaining issues in a branch” by bounding test processes and making upstream publication use a consistent repository target.
Previously receipt collection required task bookkeeping, private-repository lookup used an implicit repository, and the CLI relied on natural process exit.

Per-file execution uses `--timeout 120000` and a default 15-minute watchdog with captured output on expiry; Windows termination uses `taskkill /T /F`.
After a summary appears, a default 20-second grace period permits normal exit before killing the process and deriving success from zero fail/error counts; positive finite environment overrides configure both timers.
Killed children have their pipes destroyed and are unreferenced, source and packaged runners exit explicitly, and the CI test job has a 45-minute limit.

The CLI flushes output, optionally records its exit code in `TRACETOON_EXIT_FILE`, clears that variable before descendants inherit it, and exits explicitly; the test preload routes matching CLI spawns through a guard that kills a still-running child three seconds after its completion file appears.
Review CLI helpers redirect output to files, use a 90-second spawn cap with partial output on error, and configure a one-minute fake reviewer timeout; merged-list assertions sort reviewer labels instead of hard-coding pass order.
When a helper receives a spawn error but stdout parses as JSON, it infers status from an `error` key; otherwise it throws with partial output.
The guard and runner tests distinguish recorded completion from a command that remains unfinished.

Repository resolution prefers a valid gh default matching a remote, falls back to origin, accepts a valid default without origin, and skips gh offline.
Context and approval retain the target, preview displays it, publication rejects a changed approved target, and PR view/list/create/edit, visibility, title-rule and recent-comic lookups receive explicit targets when known.
Doctor displays the resolved target and checks origin push access; automatic private-repository attachment checks the target while comic hosting still pushes to origin.
Fork publication supplies `owner:branch` and filters existing PRs by fork owner.
Receipts count without task bookkeeping; extracted summary parsing favors wrapper stdout totals, while environment identity excludes terminal/display/temp variables but retains PATH and toolchain identity.

The comic test distinguishes searched recent-comic listings from other PR listings.

title: feat(review): simplify reviewer handoffs with lean packets
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR supports the request to “be more aggressive on parallelization” and get the work done faster by simplifying the reviewer handoff: a reviewer reads one packet and reports findings, while Tracetoon constructs the review contract. The commit message reports that full review cost about 38% of each draft, largely from reading workflow material and assembling review JSON.

`review-packet --lean --run <id>` packages the fingerprint, numbered rendered description, stored changes, commit messages, open limits, test titles and requests, hunk owners and reduced diff; `--run` defaults to the latest run and global `--json` provides structured output. Generated Validation, markers and comics are elided, and generated, lock and version files are omitted from the diff. When the reduced patch is at most 16,000 characters, its hunks are shown together; larger patches retain cited hunks, branching hunks and test assertions, with test files reduced to assertion and title lines. The lean reviewer instructions require a cold read and claim/coverage audit, allow at most three location lookups, and request at most eight consequential findings.

`review import --run <id>` validates findings schema v1 and lists errors to fix, then writes review JSON v2 bound to the current rendered input, with inline drafting and a delegated reviewer. `--findings` overrides the run’s default findings file and `--agent-id` overrides its reviewer ID; placeholder IDs are refused. Evidence resolution maps change references and paths within changed hunks into contract references; existing paths outside those hunks remain notes, and unknown references produce warnings. Omission findings without resolved diff evidence become cold-read transfer gaps. Missing guidance, unassessed guidance requirements, missing behavior checkpoints or a comic without image review leave the imported review incomplete while permitting publication. Callers therefore supply findings and a real reviewer ID rather than assembling the contract bookkeeping themselves.

The shared `evidenceExists` validator is exported for import-time reference checks.

`tests/review-lean.test.ts` covers small and large packet selection, aggregated validation errors, placeholder IDs and exact or loose quote location.

title: feat(review): run planned reviewers together and merge findings
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
To support “the next code round,” this PR makes planned reviews runnable together, with one merged list for the drafter to assess in a single edit pass.
Previously the skill directed Tracetoon-run reviews through `review run --run <id>` once per lens; it now directs one `review run --all --run <id>` invocation.

`--all` runs one review per planned lens plus general reviews beyond the lens count concurrently, with separate packet, reply, findings and reviewed-body files per slot.
On partial failure, successful reviews are imported, unsuccessful reviews are named, and the command exits nonzero with a rerun command; an ordinary rerun skips reviews imported for the current body on the verified model unless `--fresh` is supplied.
Single-review invocation without `--lens` also accepts plans requiring general reviews beyond their lenses.

The merged list deduplicates normalized and near-duplicate quotes, or quote-free findings with matching kind and evidence references; evidence accepts arrays or comma/pipe-separated strings, and fuzzy quote matching requires at least three distinct tokens in the shorter quote.
Claims with nonempty quotes absent from both current title and body are excluded and counted as fixed.
It trims quotes, keeps the strongest verdict, names contributing reviews, orders verdicts with claims before missing findings, and caps the default list at 12; `review merge` produces this list from imported reviews for the agent runner.

title: fix: recognise the VEX AIM user serial port and complete user writes
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR addresses the request to fix “the bug with the serial ports on the vex aim devices” by recognising the AIM user interface and completing writes through a dedicated user port. Previously, location-based classification used the Brain layout of interface 0 for system and 2 for user, returned `Some(empty)` when nothing matched, and the dedicated-user-port write branch returned the potentially partial result of one `write()` call without flushing.

For AIM PID `0x0700`, `types_by_location()` now classifies interface 4 as user after the existing macOS interface adjustment; the existing interface 0 and 2 classification remains available. The recognition commit explains that AIM interfaces 2–3 belong to its UVC camera, and that dropping interface 4 caused device discovery to omit the user port and user reads and writes to take the system-port fallback. When location classification recognises no ports, it now returns `None`, allowing name-based fallback discovery to run.

When a dedicated user port exists, `write_user()` now uses `write_all()`, flushes, and returns the buffer length after both operations succeed, so successful callers get a completed buffer write rather than a potentially partial count. The write commit describes this as matching the system-port send path.

Unit tests in `packages/vex-v5-serial/src/serial.rs` cover AIM interfaces 0/4, Brain interfaces 0/2, and `None` for unrecognised locations; their input helper increments interface numbers on macOS to accommodate the classifier’s subtraction. The recorded runs used Linux/x64, so they do not show the macOS-specific path running. CI results for the final head are absent from the session logs.

title: Add AIM camera snapshots and platform build artifacts
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR adds a CLI path for saving an AIM camera frame as a JPEG and makes potentially truncated execution output easier to recognize. Previously, `run` dispatched the existing commands without a `Snap` branch, and `run_exec` reported timeouts without the added truncation field or hint.

`vexaim snap` accepts `-o`/`--output`, defaulting to `vexaim-snap-<unix-time>.jpg` in the current directory. It selects cameras whose names contain “aim” case-insensitively, requests 640×480 MJPEG at 30 fps, and tries another matching camera when creation or stream opening fails. It attempts eight frame reads, keeps the latest successful frame, strips trailing zero bytes from MJPEG data, and writes the JPEG; absent matching cameras, exhausted streaming attempts, unexpected formats, and write errors produce errors. Successful captures return the path, dimensions, and byte count through JSON or human-readable output, so callers can locate the saved image. Tests in `crates/vexaim-cli/src/snap.rs` check that zero padding is trimmed and an unpadded JPEG stays unchanged. The camera comments explain the retries in terms of two video nodes with one streaming, and the repeated reads in terms of auto-exposure settling. Native camera access uses `nokhwa` with `input-native`.

Execution JSON adds `possible_output_truncation`, true when execution timed out and stdout contains at least 1500 bytes; under that same condition, human output appends advice to print less or pause between chunks.

The build workflow runs on pushes and manual dispatch, builds and tests on Linux x86_64, Windows x86_64, macOS arm64 and macOS x86_64, then uploads platform binaries with SHA256 checksums. Its setup script clones upstream if needed, fetches, checks out the pinned revision, applies the AIM patch, and prints the latest two commits. title: Add AIM REPL probes and experimental file upload tools
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR provides AIM REPL probes and experimental program-file tools; the commit describes the goal as “Find AIM REPL on USB iface 4” and reports “10/10 round trips.”
The implementation combines serial REPL scripts with system-port file commands, enabling inspection, upload, and explicit run/stop operations through separate tools.

The REPL scripts accept a port argument and open it at 115200 baud: `tests/capture.py` accepts a duration and optional lines, waits four seconds before sending them, and reads its line ending from `EOL` with a newline default.
`tests/pingpong.py` defaults to ten iterations, clears input before each attempt, and recognizes the complete PONG response and prompt rather than the echoed expression; unsuccessful attempts retain received bytes in its JSON output.
`tests/repl.py` sends CRLF-terminated expressions and prints the bytes collected by timed drains.

For file operations, the tools select the first discovered device.
The directory tool queries six vendors, continues after a count error, and reads up to 64 entries per vendor, printing entry names, sizes, load addresses, CRCs, and metadata; entry errors are printed as enumeration continues.
The loader maps `run` to the supplied filename or `slot_1.bin`, and maps `stop` to `null` under the User vendor; other action values panic.
The uploader reads a local file, constructs `slot_N.ini` and `slot_N.bin`, and uploads both to User/QSPI with `DoNothing` exit actions; the explicit `bin` argument selects Binary metadata, while other values select Vm metadata.
The loader comment associates the `null` stop filename with VAIMRC-Console.
The uploader comment describes an instructor-approved, exclusive-robot experiment and calls the format a hypothesis based on cargo-v5 PR#22 and VAIMRC-Console.
Its metadata includes the extension string, timestamp, and version 1.0.0, so uploading and starting a program remain separate operations.

The dependency enables `file-commands` alongside `serial`; reference gitlinks pin VAIMRC-Console to `b645a6ec69ad13b57b6edcb9ce60508e950b4f3c` and aim-ai to `38b1b9baf9341e77939807f2a8e3933632c21c70`, with generated artifacts including a ping-pong JSON capture and two serial transcripts.

The skill directs agents to fix diagnostic failures before proceeding and explains that `exec` supplies the robot and VEX constants automatically, reserving `--no-preamble` for deliberate use.

The instructions explain persistent REPL variables, short supervised moves and camera images that may need rotation before analysis; status examples read heading through `robot.inertial.get_heading()`. Troubleshooting maps doctor failures to cable, port contention, permissions and REPL recovery steps, with Linux-specific udev installation guidance and Windows/macOS camera-access notes. The skill distinguishes calls reported to run without error from physical effects requiring human confirmation and identifies turns, the kicker, longer/faster moves, vision on real objects, Ctrl-C during motion and unplug/replug behavior as areas still needing hardware checks.

title: Make tag search stationary and offer contact-based fast play
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Make pickup-and-delivery games quicker for children, as requested: camera checking and pauses helped testing, but routine play should make a brisk attempt and continue. This change offers explicit `verification="contact"` alongside the default `verification="vision"`, and searches tags using stationary native-camera views. Previously, pickup contact called vision confirmation and marker approach checked carried cargo regardless of verification policy.

Tag targets dispatched through `find` use up to eight stationary views separated by 45-degree turns, settling for 300 ms and sampling three times; unsuccessful samples pause 100 ms before another sample when `sample < 2`. Search stops after the eighth view or when the elapsed search reaches 20 seconds at the view boundary, subject to the shared activity deadline. `tag_turn_dps` defaults to the configured turn speed and can be set separately.

In contact mode, already-held cargo can bypass visual confirmation; acquisition accepts native possession directly or completes a bounded contact attempt without a retention reverse. During marker approach, carried-cargo loss checks apply in vision mode, and the pre-placement confirmation gate also applies in vision mode. Contact-mode delivery accepts the same activity's preceding pickup; a standalone delivery still requires possession confirmation. Assumed pickup or placement reports `completed: true` with nullable `collected`/`delivered` and explicit assumed evidence, so callers can continue effects without claiming physical confirmation.

The bundled guidance tells agents to follow contact mode when the workshop skill applies and to accept assumed completion without host camera verification; explicit diagnostic tests retain vision verification, with matching release inputs advanced to 0.5.1 from the previous 0.5.0 prerequisite. `dev/test_behaviors.py` covers stationary tag search in both directions, bounded missing-marker search, missing possession readings, contact limits, missing cargo, placement assumptions and deadlines using a simulated world.

title: Prefer SDL FreeRDP for full desktop sessions on Wayland
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
For the full Windows desktop on Wayland, prefer SDL FreeRDP while keeping the contribution a “minimal change that can easily be diffed and accepted upstream,” and cover both unversioned SDL executables and the FreeRDP Flatpak.
Previously, automatic command discovery started with `xfreerdp`, followed by the existing `xfreerdp3` and FreeRDP Flatpak discovery paths.

When `FREERDP_COMMAND` is empty, the requested mode is `windows`, and `XDG_SESSION_TYPE` is `wayland`, discovery now tries `sdl-freerdp3`, `sdl3-freerdp`, and `sdl-freerdp` in that order.
The first executable found becomes the command; accepting the unversioned name accommodates the installation described in the request, where `sdl-freerdp` refers to version 3.
If those executables are absent and Flatpak lists `com.freerdp.FreeRDP`, discovery selects `flatpak run --command=sdl-freerdp com.freerdp.FreeRDP` and marks it as a Flatpak invocation.
The command acceptance condition also recognizes that SDL Flatpak command string.

A configured `FREERDP_COMMAND` bypasses automatic discovery; when the SDL selection leaves the command empty, the existing X11-client discovery remains available.
For RemoteApp/app launches and sessions outside that Wayland desktop condition, discovery follows the existing `xfreerdp` path.
An eligible Wayland desktop launch can therefore select SDL, while app launches retain their existing automatic client preference.

The `java-6-05` launch failure motivates the request to build a harness that runs through samples in both books in order and fixes resulting bugs; this PR adds a compiled-CLI campaign with persistent book workspaces to catch shared-project checkpoint problems.

The harness walks authored steps in order, uses headless replay for external graphical launches, then checks representative Pygame and JavaFX windows.

`--binary` defaults to the current platform's `bin/aifirst-*` asset (or `bin/aifirst`), and `--report` to `test-results/book-walk/report.json`; `--book`, `--from`, `--skip-smoke`, and `--keep-workspace` control selection, starting point, smoke checks, and cleanup.

The exit status is nonzero for a step failure, blocked remaining steps, a smoke failure, or version mismatch; progress mismatch also fails an unfiltered full walk when its steps pass; non-Windows process cleanup attempts group termination before falling back to the child.

For managed project roots, checkpoint preparation removes obsolete generated files when their recorded hashes still match, forgets missing records, and refuses modified obsolete files with `checkpoint_conflict`.

Callers requesting `--relax-output` must set `AIFIRST_BOOK_WALK=1`; relaxed replay skips captured stdout/stderr comparisons while retaining exit-code and timeout expectations.

Mismatched commands expose arguments, streams, and timeout state (defaulting to false); portable removal restricts its shortcut to a single simple argument and normalizes backslashes.

When a learning launch returns an error, it shows details in a TUI card or terminal output, using a fallback failure text for empty details.

`test/native-learn.test.ts` covers launch-detail rendering; `test/e2e.test.ts` covers rejection of relaxed output outside the harness, and `test/replay-flow.test.ts` covers multi-file portable removal and relaxed matching with exit-code enforcement.

`test/run.test.ts` covers forward/reverse thermostat checkpoints and refusal to remove learner-modified obsolete files; `test:books` exposes the harness through package scripts.

The reusable Ubuntu workflow installs learner runtimes, builds the binary, runs under Xvfb, and uploads the report even after failure; PR/main CI calls it and releases depend on it.

title: fix: use Homebrew for Maven on immutable Linux
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Fix Maven installation for the reported `java-11-01` failure on Bazzite, addressing the request to detect an immutable distribution and install through Homebrew instead.
Previously, Maven installation planning supported Homebrew on macOS and native Linux package managers including APT, DNF, and Alpine apk, without the immutable-Linux branch introduced here.

The new `isImmutableLinux` helper checks for Linux together with either `/run/ostree-booted` or an available `rpm-ostree` command.
Its command lookup defaults to `Bun.which`, normalizing a missing executable to `undefined`, and both executable lookup and file existence can be supplied by callers.
For Maven planning on a detected immutable Linux system, `systemDependencyInstallPlan` resolves Homebrew before considering the native Linux package-manager branches and uses the resolved executable path for `brew install maven`.
If Homebrew is missing in that branch, the planner returns no installation plan instead of falling through to DNF.

When no plan is available and all missing system dependencies are Maven on detected immutable Linux, `installDependencies` returns guidance to install Homebrew, put `brew` on PATH, and retry.

title: fix: make Claude integration independent of CLI PATH

Windows Claude Code sessions could fail with `aifirst: command not found` in both the replay hook and ordinary exercise commands; this PR implements the requested “complete Claude Code integration independent of the parent process’s `PATH`” using a Claude-owned Bash launcher that forwards to the current executable. Permission detection and bookmode preapproval require the launcher-based entries to be present, so existing users receive the migration through skill installation; replay documentation includes the installation command. title: fix: defer macOS setup outside the piped installer

Missing confirmation, timeout, abnormal termination, or a nonzero runner exit causes failure, and the shell assertions require the prompt to follow installer completion.

CI retains its Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows check matrix and adds the smoke test to the Darwin build-and-smoke branch; the shellcheck job includes the new shell script.
