Existing nonempty fixtures require `--replace`, preventing an accidental overwrite during routine capture. Subprocess errors stop capture unless failure was explicitly allowed; Showtail verification accepts its specifically recognized exit-3 raw-event validation gap and rejects other nonzero results. Canonical-event or source differences also reject the capture before publishing the staged fixture; failures retain the capture workspace, while success removes it unless `AIFIRST_KEEP_CLAUDE_E2E_CAPTURE` is set.

Previously exact planning matches called planning directly, and the selected replay path returned its planning outcome without attaching trailing pre-plan text. Exact workflow matches with planning enabled now use the shared selected-replay path, which retains text-only preambles when it begins planning without pre-plan segments; `test/planning.test.ts` covers the preamble before the first question.

Long-running learner commands should not freeze rendering: this implements the requested “TUI Quality-of-Life Improvements” by keeping terminal programs inside the TUI with live output and embedded reader input. Previously, asynchronous replay command execution fell through to the synchronous executor, and prompt cancellation released animation waits without a corresponding reveal state.

Exercise execution shares an asynchronous process runner that captures stdout/stderr while forwarding chunks, supplies authored input through a pipe, and exposes writable input when interactive input is requested. Reader mode on the final interactive command uses the embedded input callback when supplied, otherwise inherited stdin; execution stops after a nonzero exit, timeout, or abort, and `--no-timeout` disables execution timeouts. Interactive steps lacking authored stdin require a terminal in the CLI path, and empty output gets an explicit completion message in text mode. Aborted learner runs report “Program stopped”; Windows termination uses `taskkill`, while Unix termination attempts the process group with a direct-process fallback.

During prompt animation, a keypress or prompt click reveals the text and ends the animation wait without also running the prompt; proposed-plan rendering enables any-key skipping across the document. Choosing Run resumes bottom-following, and detailed pickers use compact scrollable panels with Page Up/Page Down navigation when a detail scroller exists. The TUI also waits 40 ms before clearing the program panel for the next screen.

Asynchronous replay commands resolve `<python>`, respect the operation’s working directory and stdin, and skip graphical launches on Linux when neither display variable exists. PNG signatures produce dimensions and byte-count metadata; NUL bytes or invalid UTF-8 produce file-type metadata instead of binary text; the release version becomes 0.13.4. `test/replay-flow.test.ts` covers event-loop progress, timeouts, and PNG metadata; `test/graphical-run.test.ts` covers embedded input/output, while `test/tui-streaming.test.ts` covers reveal and resumed following.

`test/terminal-renderer.test.ts` checks reveal without also running the prompt, and `test/tui-choice.test.ts` checks compact pickers. `test/run.test.ts` checks that reader input yields “Hello, Ada!” instead of “Hello, Sushi!”; `test/tui-learn.test.ts` covers embedded exercise input and the scrollable PocketCFO default.

title: fix: make Python replays portable across platforms
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Python replays need a portable execution description while retaining the captured tool label and command for playback; this PR separates those concerns in the content and importer.
Previously imported shell operations stored the captured command as `bash -lc`, and status text combined the tool name with a description, name, or prompt when present.

When imported source paths include a `.py` file, shell operations retain their captured argv and gain a `portableCommand` beginning with `<shell>`.
The portable command replaces `python3` with `<python>` for the recognized version, inline-code, module, and Python-file invocation forms.
Display metadata takes the captured tool name, falling back to `Tool`, and includes description and command when those strings are nonempty.
The replay types and schema accept display metadata on operations and status events, with a required `toolName` inside that metadata; command operations also accept portable argv and timeout expectations.

For Python steps, validation propagates the portability requirement through replay operations, normal events, pre-plan events, workflow interludes, and variant operations and events.
A captured `bash` command containing the checked Python, removal, timeout, listing, or environment-assignment patterns must provide a portable command beginning with `<shell>`.
Validation also rejects empty portable argv and timeout expectations without a nonzero `timeoutMs`, so malformed replay descriptions fail content validation.

The Python content supplies portable commands such as `<python> --version; <python> -c "import pygame; print(pygame.ver)"` alongside captured Bash and PowerShell display labels; the package version changes from `1.7.1` to `1.7.2`.
The generated Rocket Python fixture also carries the replay metadata.
The chapter 9–10 audit tests check portable execution for captured shell commands and separation of the original Windows tool label from execution.

The privacy-equivalence comparison excludes `display` and `portableCommand`; the importer expectation includes portable shell argv and the captured Bash display command.

The captured Python progression now records references from `py-9-02` through `py-10-04` to their preceding exercise scaffolds, including `py-10-01` to `py-9-03`. This gives consumers an explicit starting-scaffold reference for dependent replays; content validation rejects a supplied reference when its exercise is unknown or its scaffold contains no files.

It describes that extra step as temporary and explains that guided setup selects a book, creates a learning workspace, and offers to start the built-in learner.

The installer comment attributes the terminal-input issue to Bun reopening macOS’s `/dev/tty` alias and points to `oven-sh/bun#41495`; the workaround avoids that setup invocation on the `darwin` path without adding a replacement terminal-detection mechanism.

title: fix(digest): ignore commands quoted inside scripts and heredocs
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
To support the request, “Can you dogfood this and use it for a PR,” this PR fixes command detection that mistakes inline script text for executed tests. Previously command detection split on shell separators and newlines inside quotes and heredoc bodies, so an inline mention of `bun test` could be classified as an executed test and produce a grouping key such as `bun test',`. A shared `splitCommands` helper now feeds test detection, command grouping, and commit detection, preserving quoted script text and skipping recognized heredoc bodies.

The splitter recognizes single quotes, double quotes, and backticks, and preserves escaped characters outside single quotes when a following character exists. Outside those quoted or escaped spans, it separates chains and pipelines at `&&`, `||`, semicolons, pipes, and newlines. When a supported heredoc marker has a following newline, it skips the body through a delimiter line recognized by its LF-based matcher (allowing surrounding spaces or tabs), or through the end of the input when a delimiter is absent; commands after a matched delimiter remain available for detection. This lets callers distinguish an inline script containing test names from a separate test command following that script.

`commandKey` continues to bypass leading setup segments such as `cd` and now filters tokens beginning with heredoc or redirection prefixes alongside flags before selecting the program and first argument. `tests/shell.test.ts` covers chains and pipes, quoted scripts, heredoc bodies and following commands, test-runner mentions inside scripts, and grouping from the first real command; the release metadata advances from 1.0.0-rc.11 to 1.0.0-rc.12.

To address the request to “see if summaries are being generated properly,” this PR tightens digest attribution and puts the underlying evidence beside the description, so dogfooding real Tracetoon changes exposes mistakes reviewers can inspect.

Previously, committed work used a window ending 30 minutes after the last commit, or the current time for a dirty checkout; command failures depended on `isError`, and shared sessions could relate PRs into a saga.

Recognized test commands use the runner segment as their label, and failures include recognized failure text in output, allowing piped failures and subsequent recovery milestones to appear. Claude tool results marked as errors preserve nonempty, nonsynthetic “the user said” text as feedback that continues the turn. Saga relationships retain stacked-branch and explicit-link conditions, removing shared sessions as a sufficient condition. Explicit `head` options support historical comparisons without using working-tree changes.

The preview presents digest facts, prompts, plans, decisions, tests, milestones and disclosure in a styled Evidence panel; the writing guide requires claim-by-claim checks, digest-backed numbers and plan approvals, and the user's word for events outside the logs. title: Support lean comparison runs and cross-model composite deltas
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
The request to “prune any variations” while finding a default with equal or higher composite quality at much lower cost motivates leaner comparison runs and a cross-model composite view. This PR lets callers omit native writers while keeping the baseline–candidate comparison, and exposes composite differences alongside error-rate differences to support that evaluation. `compare --systems` accepts comma-separated `native`, `baseline`, and `candidate` aliases, full Tracetoon names, and the selected provider’s native name; omitted or empty selections default to all three systems. Selection uses the provider’s canonical order and rejects unknown names or selections missing baseline or candidate; the code comment identifies the baseline pairing as the primary comparison. Without native, writers exclude that system and candidate-versus-baseline judgments run in both orders. Planned counts, rebuild coverage, the quality gate, and `--plan` output follow the selected systems, so callers can reduce the matrix without requiring native comparison results.

Subset selections are recorded in manifest settings and participate in experiment identity; selecting all three omits that setting, preserving the previous identity shape. A resume without `--systems` keeps the frozen selection, and manifests without a systems setting fall back to the provider’s full system list. `tests/comparison.test.ts` covers planning without native, completing and scoring that selection, and recording its systems for resume; these tests use a fake comparison setup rather than the real comparison setup.

When candidate and baseline arms have shared cases, the accuracy table includes candidate-minus-baseline composite deltas computed from per-case means with a case-clustered 95% bootstrap interval. `tests/score.test.ts` checks cross-model case clustering and a reproducible interval.

title: Judge saved candidate drafts against baselines from another run
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
The approved plan to “confirm the Haiku win, cut its cost, close the last gaps” identified that its composite comparison relied on separate runs; this PR provides direct pairwise judging across runs using saved drafts. The `crossjudge` command pairs `tracetoon-candidate` artifacts from one comparison with `tracetoon-baseline` artifacts from another, so different writer models can be compared without rerunning writers.

Callers supply `--candidate`, `--baseline` and `--out`; optional `--cache` defaults to `.prbench-cache/v2` beside the output directory, `--parallel` defaults to four concurrent judge pairs, and `--plan` verifies inputs and reports planned calls without calling models. The CLI rejects nonpositive or noninteger parallelism, requires Claude authentication outside planning mode, and sets exit code 2 for errors caught by its action handler. Previously the existing cleanup command set exit code 1 when cleanup remained pending; that behavior remains separate from crossjudge's error handling.

Both input manifests must name exactly one writer model and agree on judges, rubric version, judge contract, replicate count, split and case IDs/hashes; the current harness must also match the rubric and contract. Draft identities and receipts are checked before judging, so a missing draft aborts before judge calls are spent. Compatible pairs are judged in both orders by each configured judge and summarized with compare's consensus rule, alongside per-draft composite scores and numeric stored judgment costs. `--out` receives `pairs.json`, `summary.json` and a Markdown summary with per-case, per-side and replicate/case rows.

Saved judgments can be reused on reruns, and an output directory containing different crossjudge provenance is refused.

`tests/crossjudge.test.ts` covers cross-run pairing and consensus, incompatible manifests, and missing drafts; these tests use fake judges rather than real judge providers.

body:

Timed-out judge calls can interrupt comparisons, while Codex usage needs to include delegated work for useful cost comparisons; this PR retries recoverable judge failures and makes cost coverage explicit.
Previously, the judge retry loop continued for transient failures but stopped on timeouts, and score collection descended into judgment attempt folders.

Timeouts and transient failures now share a three-attempt budget with backoff, including persisted failures on resume; cancellation stops further retries, and Codex judges report process timeouts explicitly.
Judge-attempt metadata includes judge identity; `collectJudgeFailures` gathers timeout, transient, format and other errors per judge, and `scoreMarkdown` renders the reliability table in score and rebuilt comparison reports when errors exist, using a sibling judgment or folder name for legacy identity.
This lets recoverable judge failures proceed toward a usable judgment while retaining their reliability cost in the comparison report.

Live Codex runs prefer newly created sandbox rollouts when their input-token total covers stdout usage, otherwise retaining main-thread counts when available.
Rollout accounting deduplicates response IDs across replayed histories and records usage scope and subagent counts.
For Codex artifacts without a reported cost, scoring uses recorded all-thread usage or sufficiently complete saved traces selected through the receipt's writer-attempt key, falling back to main-thread usage when available; cost estimates use the selected tokens, and tables identify coverage and mean subagents across drafts with known counts.
Scoring skips judgment attempt folders to avoid counting accepted copies of final judgments twice; per-case deltas compare candidate with same-model baseline, and paired results include a leave-one-case-out range with at least two cases having finite deltas.

Writer identity excludes shell and session bookkeeping for Codex and Claude, while a matching frozen legacy hash remains usable.
Previously, isolation proofs saved a bare model while resume compared it with the effort-qualified arm, rejecting that mismatch; probes now include the full arm, and older proofs may match the bare model while experiment, system and probe-success checks remain.

`tests/codex-usage.test.ts` covers replay deduplication, live all-thread usage and saved-trace costing; `tests/recovery.test.ts` covers persisted timeouts within the retry budget.
`tests/environment-hash.test.ts` covers shell-independent identity and legacy hash compatibility, `tests/score.test.ts` covers reliability and robustness tables, and `tests/claude-comparison.test.ts` covers saved effort-arm proofs on resume.

title: Gate performance on paired priced cost per draft
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
A candidate with more cached input can be slower while costing less; this PR makes the performance gate cost-based so that trade-off can pass. Previously the gate required improved median paired writer time and no increase in median input tokens per model. The replacement compares candidate/baseline priced cost for matching model, case and replicate, averages log ratios within each case and then across cases, and uses a threshold of at most 1.000. The case-clustered 95% interval is descriptive rather than a pass requirement.

The shared `draftCost` helper extracts the scoring calculation so comparison rebuilding and `collectDraftScores` use the same pricing path: reported totals when available, otherwise estimated token cost with per-model prices and a separate cached-input rate. For Codex estimates, it uses all-thread artifact usage when marked available, otherwise saved trace usage when sufficient; a main-thread estimate is rejected by the performance gate. Matched pairs with missing, nonfinite or nonpositive priced costs are listed with reasons and make the gate inconclusive. Missing pairs, insufficient independent cases and required work evidence still affect conclusiveness, while validation-comparability handling retains its existing conditions.

For benchmark users, cheaper candidates can therefore pass despite slower writer time or higher token counts, which remain informational; pricier candidates fail the cost criterion when usable priced data is present. `tests/performance.test.ts` covers those trade-offs, clustering repeats by case, the missing-price outcome and the stated threshold. The comparison summary prints the cost rule and ratio, labels the writer ratio informational, and lists unpriced drafts; `tests/comparison.test.ts` checks the v3 schema, summary labels and priced costs in writer metrics.

The README and changelog describe the cost criterion and `prbench.performance/v3` report schema.

title: Measure draft quality and cost across writer effort arms
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
To make graph benefits measurable beyond “A or B better,” this PR adds absolute draft scores and cost comparisons, while supporting experiments with cheaper writers and lower reasoning effort. Previously writers received `opts.model` with a fixed `medium` effort; writers now receive the parsed model and selected effort, defaulting to `medium` for bare model specs.

`prbench score <roots…>` reads saved judgments, with `--cases` or `--dataset` selecting fact sheets and `--json` emitting per-draft records; compare summaries include the same score view. It averages applicable judgments per draft, reports claim/context/uncertainty coverage and rubric components, and combines them on a 0–100 scale: weights 35/15/15/35, minus 15 per factual error, 7 per unsupported claim and 10 per trap, floored at zero. Arm summaries use case-clustered bootstrap intervals and paired candidate deltas; an Accuracy view compares candidate and baseline arms on shared cases, reporting the share of judgments finding factual errors with case-clustered 95% intervals, validation/code structure/attribution/motivation/pipeline/other error classes, a 0.05 claim-coverage guard and cost ratios where positive costs exist. Reported USD takes precedence; when absent, known-model token counts can supply an estimate with cached input priced separately.

`compare --models model@effort` validates distinct specs against provider-supported efforts; explicit-effort artifacts must match both fields, while bare specs match the model without constraining effort. Isolation probes check skill loading using the bare model and configured probe effort; the commit message reports that Haiku@low path misreports had stopped runs. Writers classified as no-draft, scope-rejected or timed-out can retry up to three attempts unless cancelled; scope audit precedes cache insertion, and failure records identify the arm.

The reliability table in `prbench score` and compare summaries counts scored drafts and no-draft, scope-rejected, timed-out and other attempts by arm. A scope-rejected draft stays rejected and excluded from scoring; retries avoid its rejected cache entry, and the commit message describes a fresh sandbox per sample. Fake GitHub supports commit-derived `--fill`, `--fill-first` and `--fill-verbose`, with explicit title/body taking precedence.

The no-draft handling addresses low-effort writers finishing without a PR: the commit message reports Luna refusing to publish and Sonnet using `gh pr create --fill`, previously captured without a title, both invalidating runs.

`tests/arm.test.ts` covers parsing, provider validation and artifact matching; `tests/score.test.ts` covers components, penalties, cost, aggregation and reliability. `tests/comparison.test.ts` records a simulated scope rejection and `tests/sandbox.test.ts` checks commit-derived fill titles; these use fake collaborators rather than real providers.

title: fix: recover shell exit codes from Claude result text
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
To support the request to use the chapter 9 exercises as acceptance criteria, the importer now recovers shell exit codes carried in Claude tool-result text, helping the importer preserve information needed to compare captured Claude output with replay verification.

Previously, `rawToolResult` obtained exit codes from integer-valued `exitCode`, `exit_code`, or `code` fields in the structured result or tool-result block. It now falls back to parsing the block's `content` when neither source supplies an integer exit code; structured fields retain precedence over block fields, and both retain precedence over text.

The new `resultTextExitCode` helper accepts a string beginning with `Exit code ` followed by an optionally negative integer and a newline or the end of the string. A missing or empty string, or content without that leading status line, yields no parsed exit code; after conversion, the helper returns the number when `Number.isInteger` accepts it and otherwise returns `undefined`. This lets consumers of the resulting tool event receive an exit status from that text format when the numeric fields are absent, while preserving the existing field-based selection.

title: feat: upgrade installed Showtail without rerunning the installer
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Installed Showtail users need a way to update without finding and rerunning the installer; this PR implements the request to “Make a showtail upgrade command to upgrade showtail from an install so users don’t have to re-run the installer.” Previously, the CLI routed integration operations such as `undo` and rejected incompatible session options through its existing command handling; it now also exposes `showtail upgrade` in a maintenance help group, with `--json` for machine-readable output.

The updater checks the latest GitHub Release, compares numeric version triples, and selects the binary asset for supported Linux/macOS x64 or arm64 builds and Windows x64 builds. A Bun/source invocation is refused before requesting release information, to avoid replacing the Bun runtime, so callers using a source checkout must keep using their package or Git workflow. For an installed version matching the release, the command reports that it is current; when the installed version is newer, it reports that fact without replacing files.

When an update is available, it downloads the executable and bundled extension, verifies the executable’s reported version before replacement, and stages backups for recovery if replacement fails. On Windows it schedules a detached PowerShell helper to wait for the running command to exit before swapping files and silently invoking `setup --first-run --json`, and reports a pending update; on Linux/macOS replacement happens in the command, followed by an integration refresh attempt. If that refresh does not succeed, the command tells users integrations will refresh on the next Showtail run; the documentation now directs installed users to the upgrade command.

`tests/cli.test.ts` checks refusal of source invocations; `tests/selfUpgrade.test.ts` checks asset mapping, version comparisons, Windows helper construction, replacement, current-version handling, and file preservation on verification errors, and restoration of both installed files if replacement is interrupted.

This puts the platform selection in one place for both installers while preserving their `--install-extension` and `--force` arguments: VS Code supplies its selected payload, and Antigravity supplies its bundled VSIX.

Callers therefore use the same Windows invocation path for a bare launcher name or an explicit launcher path.

title: Clarify behavior ownership and code-change direction in PR evidence
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR implements the request to “implement both fixes and rerun Claude and Codex”: give description writers explicit behavior ownership and change direction, so they can place a behavior and distinguish removed code from additions. Previously code cells displayed raw `+`/`-` lines, and conflict extraction recognized paired changes using the literal separator `  ⇒  + `.

Changed-line words are recorded per function, with a changed doc comment assigned to the definition below it. `ownerRows` in `src/graph/briefExtras.ts` matches commit-sentence clauses against those words, discounts words shared across functions, rewards linked hunks, and requires a clear lead. For linked sentences, candidates come from the linked hunks’ files; otherwise changed source functions face a higher threshold. Ownership rows require separate matches with distinct function sets within the same file and change unit, with at most five rows per unit and six overall; they describe ownership rather than call relationships. When present, these pointers appear in the TOON output, neighborhood tail and lean review packet, including lens A.

Code cells spell out `added:`, `removed:` and `was … → now …`; matched boolean-condition changes, including multiline chains, identify dropped, kept and added operands instead of repeating consumed fragments. Value fallbacks such as `a || ref` remain value changes, and `added:`/`removed:` labels receive a budget adjustment so their expanded wording does not increase their cost. Drafting guidance directs writers to read direction from code cells and take behavior locations from ownership pointers. Conflict extraction accepts whitespace around the arrow and before the plus sign, and ownership pointers are excluded when calculating the search-evidence budget.

For maintainers, this separates where a behavior lives from which way its condition changed.

`tests/brief-owners-direction.test.ts` covers per-function words, doc-comment assignment, sentence ownership, ambiguous or missing ownership data, clause splitting and lean-packet pointers; its direction assertions cover operand splitting, condition changes, value fallbacks and code-cell rendering.

`tests/brief-extras.test.ts` supplies `fnWords` in its fixture, and `tests/graph-search.test.ts` expects the explicit `added:` prefix.

title: fix: bound CLI test hangs and preserve fork PR targets
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Windows checks running for hours motivate the request “Is the windows check hung? 3 hours.”; this PR bounds stalled test processes and makes upstream publication from forks use a resolved repository.
Previously receipt collection required task bookkeeping, PR creation supplied the bare branch, and the file harness waited for the child’s close event without a limit.

Target resolution uses gh’s default when it matches a clone remote, falls back to origin when that default is stale, and accepts a valid default when origin is absent; offline resolution skips gh.
Context records that target, render includes it in approval and its code and prints it, and publish refuses a changed target before posting when approval records a repository.
PR, recent-comic and title-rule lookups name the resolved repository; existing-PR lookup qualifies the head when origin and target owners differ; doctor reports the target and checks push access against origin when available, while automatic comic attachment checks target visibility and image hosting still pushes to origin.
Fork creation uses `--head owner:branch` when origin and target owners differ, and reconciliation filters by head owner in that case; `tests/flow.test.ts` checks target pinning and refusal after a target change.
Receipts are read when present without `task begin`; extracted summary parsing favors wrapper totals on stdout, and environment identity ignores terminal and temporary-directory variables matched by `VOLATILE_VARS` while retaining PATH sensitivity.

The harness uses `--timeout 120000`, a per-test timeout, plus a default 15-minute file watchdog, and a 20-second post-summary grace period (both watchdog and grace accept positive millisecond environment overrides); after that grace, the runner kills the child and uses failure/error counts, while an unfinished file fails with partial output.
Windows termination invokes `taskkill /T /F`; settled runners destroy pipes and unref children, source and packaged runners flush and exit explicitly, and CI test jobs have a 45-minute limit.
The CLI flushes output, optionally records its exit code, clears the exit-file variable before dispatch, and exits explicitly; the test preload routes matching CLI spawns through a guard that kills a still-running child three seconds after its completion file appears.
Review tests redirect output to files, cap calls at 90000ms and fake reviewers at 60000ms, and accept complete JSON after a subprocess error; otherwise they report partial output.
The merged-list assertion accepts completion-dependent pass order; the shipped bundle is rebuilt.
`tests/receipts-and-fork.test.ts` checks fork heads, receipts, summaries and environment identity; `tests/target.test.ts` checks target selection.
`tests/spawn-guard.test.ts` checks exit codes and unfinished hangs; `tests/test-files.test.ts` checks watchdog failure and summary-derived outcomes.

title: fix: recognise VEX AIM user serial ports and complete user writes
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Fix the serial-port bug on VEX AIM devices, addressing the request to “submit the PR to the vex-v5-serial project for the bug with the serial ports on the vex aim devices.” The change recognises AIM interface 4 as a user port and completes buffered writes when a dedicated user port is present. Previously, according to the AIM commit, location-based discovery knew the Brain layout (interfaces 0 and 2) and returned `Some(empty)` when nothing matched; the removed dedicated-port branch of `write_user()` returned a single `write()` result.

For AIM PID `0x0700`, `types_by_location()` classifies interface 4 as `User` before the existing location match; the interface 0 system mapping and interface 2 user mapping remain available through that match. The AIM commit explains that interfaces 2 and 3 belong to its UVC camera and that dropping interface 4 caused user reads and writes to take the system-port fallback. When location-based discovery recognises no ports, it now returns `None`; the AIM commit identifies this as allowing name-based discovery fallbacks to run.

A single write may accept part of a buffer, as the write commit explains. When `self.user_port` is present, `write_user()` awaits `write_all()` and `flush()` before returning the full buffer length, propagating errors from either operation. Callers using that branch therefore receive the full length after both operations succeed rather than a possibly partial write count.

The added regression cases check AIM interfaces 0/4, Brain interfaces 0/2, and `None` for an unrecognised location in `packages/vex-v5-serial/src/serial.rs`. Their helper adds one on macOS; the AIM commit explains that serialport reports the CDC data interface one above the communication interface and `types_by_location()` subtracts one there. The recorded runs were on Linux/x64, so they do not show the macOS path running. CI results for the final head are absent from the session logs.

title: Add AIM REPL probes and experimental file upload tools
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
This PR provides AIM REPL probing scripts and experimental file tools for inspecting, uploading, and loading programs over the serial connection. The Python probes accept an explicit serial port so callers can target the REPL connection.

`tests/pingpong.py` defaults to ten attempts and sends a Python expression whose echoed source differs from the expected PONG output. It recognizes success when the response includes the output and prompt, returns a timeout result otherwise, and emits JSON with individual timings and successful-trip latency statistics. `tests/capture.py` reads for a caller-supplied duration and, when lines are supplied, sends them after four seconds with an `EOL` environment override; `tests/repl.py` sends CRLF-terminated expressions and drains replies for fixed intervals.

The Rust tools use the first discovered device and the `Connection` trait, with `file-commands` enabled alongside `serial` on the local `vex-v5-serial` dependency. The loader accepts `run` or `stop`: run defaults to `slot_1.bin`, while stop sends the filename `null` to vendor User. The uploader’s source labels its format a hypothesis based on cargo-v5 PR#22 and VAIMRC-Console, and marks the tool for instructor-approved use with an exclusive robot.

The uploader constructs extension metadata using `FixedString`, writes a generated slot INI followed by the input bytes as `slot_N.bin` to User QSPI, and requests `DoNothing` after each transfer. Its optional type selects Binary for `bin` and Vm otherwise, leaving program execution to a separate action. Directory inspection visits six vendors, continues after a count error, and limits entry requests to 64 per vendor.

Reference gitlinks pin VAIMRC-Console at `b645a6e` and aim-ai at `38b1b9b`; generated artifacts include serial captures, round-trip JSON, and the dependency lockfile.

title: Clarify robot disconnects and document USB replug recovery

Make supervised USB replug testing actionable and retry the kicker test requested alongside the warning that the robot was sitting upside down. title: Support brisk contact-based play and stationary tag search
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
Support the requested brisk, assume-and-continue pickup and tag-delivery games for children. Pair opt-in `verification="contact"` with stationary tag search, distinguishing assumed completion from native evidence. Previously collection required possession confirmation and a retention reverse, and delivery required release confirmation before returning success.

The code comment attributes stationary search to real AIM acquisition after a continuous sweep missed the marker.

Tag targets now use up to eight stationary viewpoints separated by 45-degree turns, with a 300 ms settle and three native readings spaced 100 ms apart; another viewpoint is attempted unless the eighth view or the 20-second search bound has been reached, subject to the shared deadline. `tag_turn_dps` defaults to `turn_dps` and controls travel between views; tag reacquisition pauses before reading, while cargo search retains its continuous sweep.

Contact mode accepts an already-held cargo reading, skips the retention reverse, and permits a locally timed-out contact stroke after confirming stop. During marker approach, possession-loss checks apply when carrying cargo in vision mode; contact-mode delivery can use the same activity's remembered pickup, while standalone delivery still requires confirmed cargo. Placement and backing away can complete with `collected` or `delivered` null and explicit assumed evidence instead of claiming physical confirmation. Missing targets and whole-activity deadlines still stop the sequence; default vision mode retains diagnostic checks.

The bundled skill directs agents to follow workshop contact settings when applicable and to report assumed completion without requiring host camera verification; callers wanting diagnostic confirmation should retain vision mode. README and release guidance describe these policies and limitations alongside the matching 0.5.0-to-0.5.1 release update.

`dev/test_behaviors.py` covers stationary views in both directions, absent markers, missing possession readings, bounded contact, assumed release and deadlines; these tests use a simulated world rather than real hardware.

Hardware notes report that the final source follow-up did not reacquire blue during a bounded search; full 0.5.1 hardware acceptance remains pending.

Short native motions receive a minimum 1500 ms local limit, returning early on completion while remaining subject to the activity deadline.

title: Prefer SDL FreeRDP for full desktop mode on Wayland
body:
<!-- tracetoon:start -->
For full Windows desktop launches on Wayland, this PR prefers the SDL FreeRDP client while keeping the contribution small enough to review upstream, as requested: “prefer the simplest change that will get the intended result.” The requested compatibility cases include an unversioned `sdl-freerdp` executable and the FreeRDP Flatpak, rather than assuming that installations expose `sdl-freerdp3`. Previously, automatic command selection began with `xfreerdp`, then considered `xfreerdp3` and the FreeRDP Flatpak's X11 command.

In `waGetFreeRDPCommand`, when `FREERDP_COMMAND` is empty, the launch argument is `windows`, and `XDG_SESSION_TYPE` is `wayland`, command discovery checks `sdl-freerdp3`, `sdl3-freerdp`, and `sdl-freerdp` in that order. If those executables are absent but Flatpak is available and lists `com.freerdp.FreeRDP`, it selects `flatpak run --command=sdl-freerdp com.freerdp.FreeRDP` and sets `RDP_FLATPAK=1`. The final command acceptance condition also recognizes that SDL Flatpak command string.

The startup call now forwards its first argument into command selection, so the desktop launch mode can control this preference. A configured command bypasses automatic selection; if SDL discovery leaves the command empty, the existing X11 discovery path remains available. RemoteApp/app launches and sessions that do not meet the desktop-on-Wayland condition continue using the existing xfreerdp path. For desktop users meeting that condition with `FREERDP_COMMAND` empty, an available SDL client therefore takes precedence over the X11 clients, including when SDL is supplied through the FreeRDP Flatpak.
